c.tagline: India's spiritual heart on the Ganges — eternal ghats, dawn prayers, and the fire of the Ganga Aarti.

taxi.fareNote: Autos and taxis rarely use meters; agree the fare before boarding, or book via Uber/Ola for a fixed price. No vehicle reaches the ghats — the last stretch is on foot or by cycle-rickshaw.

emergency.note: 112 is India's single all-services emergency number; 108 reaches ambulance services and 100 the police.

avoid.reason: Pushy touts/fake guides at the ghats; caution in crowded lanes; boat-price scams

hood_desc: The tangled old-city core: Godowlia's crossroads feed the lane-maze down to Dashashwamedh Ghat, where the nightly Ganga Aarti is held, and to the Kashi Vishwanath temple. No cars reach the ghats, so expect narrow galis, cows and non-stop energy. Best for first-timers who want to be steps from the river.

The relaxed southern end of the ghat stretch, Assi is Varanasi's backpacker and yoga hub, with riverside cafes, guesthouses, morning subah-e-banaras music and a younger, bohemian feel while still on the Ganges.
Varanasi Cantonment is the leafy, orderly area around the main railway station, home to most of the city's larger and heritage hotels; a comfortable, less chaotic base a short ride from the ghats.
A modern commercial district of malls, showrooms, multiplexes and many of the city's better restaurants; practical and contemporary rather than atmospheric.

A quiet, green pilgrimage town about 10 km north where the Buddha gave his first sermon: the Dhamek Stupa, monastery ruins and the Sarnath museum. Calm and spread out, suited to a slower, spiritual stay.

water.note: Drink only bottled or filtered water and avoid ice and raw washed produce.

transit.hours: Buses and shared autos run roughly 6:00 AM to 10:00 PM; ride apps and cycle-rickshaws fill the late-night gap. Sunrise boats set out from around 5:00 AM.
transit.note: Varanasi has no metro or tram. Auto-rickshaws, e-rickshaws and cycle-rickshaws are the main way around; the old-city lanes near the ghats are too narrow for cars, so the final stretch is always on foot. Wooden and motorised boats ply the Ganges for sunrise rides and river crossings.
transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash and are almost always negotiated, not metered — agree the price before you board. Booking an auto through Uber or Ola gives a fixed fare.

bus: UPSRTC intercity buses to Lucknow, Prayagraj (Allahabad) and Gorakhpur

transit.m: Airport/city bus toward Varanasi Cantt (~60-75 min)
Prepaid taxi to the ghats (45-60 min)

tip.r: Not customary; rounding up or leaving 5-10% at nicer restaurants is appreciated. Boatmen and guides expect a negotiated tip.

food.name: Kachori Sabzi
food.desc: The Banarasi breakfast: flaky lentil-stuffed kachoris deep-fried to order and served with a spiced potato-and-pumpkin curry, often with jalebi.

places.name: Ram Bhandar
places.note: Century-old sweet shop locals queue at from dawn for kachori, jalebi and malaiyo in winter.

places.name: Kachori Gali
places.note: Whole lane of kachori-sabzi stalls frying from before sunrise; most sell out by late morning.

places.name: Shri Vishwanath Kachori Bhandar
places.note: Busy corner stall with fast turnover, so kachoris come straight out of the kadhai.

food.name: Tamatar Chaat
food.desc: Varanasi's own chaat: tomatoes mashed and simmered with spices, then piled into a clay bowl with crushed samosa, sev and lemon.

places.name: Kashi Chat Bhandar
places.note: The reference point for tamatar chaat in Banaras; crowded from late afternoon onward.

places.name: Deena Chat Bhandar
places.note: Long-running rival to Kashi, favoured by locals for a spicier, tangier version.

places.name: Vishwanath Chat Bhandar
places.note: Student-district branch of the chaat tradition, cheaper and open later into the evening.

food.name: Malaiyo
food.desc: A winter-only cloud of milk foam whipped through cold nights, dusted with saffron, cardamom and pistachio. Sold at dawn, November to February.

places.name: Chaukhamba Gali vendors
places.note: The traditional malaiyo lane; vendors set up on winter mornings and are gone by mid-morning.

places.name: Ram Bhandar
places.note: Reliable shopfront source if you would rather not chase the roaming handcart vendors.

places.name: Kshirsagar Sweets
places.note: Old sweet house that serves malaiyo in season alongside classic Banarasi mithai.

food.name: Baati Chokha
food.desc: Rustic Purvanchal plate of wheat dough balls baked over cow-dung cakes, cracked open with ghee and eaten with smoked aubergine-tomato mash.

places.name: Baati Chokha Restaurant
places.note: Village-themed sit-down institution built entirely around the baati chokha thali.

places.name: Kashi Baati Chokha
places.note: Popular local dining hall doing unlimited baati, chokha, dal and litti.

places.name: Vishalakshi Baati Chokha
places.note: Simple neighbourhood spot with the wood-fired smoky flavour done properly.

food.name: Chura Matar
food.desc: A cold-season specialty of flattened rice slow-tossed in ghee with green peas, ginger and khoya, rich and faintly sweet.

places.name: Ram Bhandar
places.note: Serves chura matar through the winter months alongside its kachori counter.

places.name: Kachori Gali stalls
places.note: Seasonal handcarts here ladle chura matar straight from the kadhai in winter mornings.

places.name: Deena Chat Bhandar
places.note: Adds chura matar to the chaat menu in season; good place to try it sitting down.

food.name: Banarasi Paan
food.desc: The city's edible full stop: tender betel leaf folded around gulkand, saunf and sweet spices. Ask for meetha (sweet), skip the tobacco.

places.name: Keshav Tambul Bhandar
places.note: Famous paan counter near the ghats, known for elaborate meetha and chocolate paans.

places.name: Kesar Paan Bhandar
places.note: Well-known university-area paanwala using proper Banarasi maghai leaf.

places.name: Paan shops of Chowk
places.note: Dozens of hereditary paanwalas in one lane; point at what regulars order.

food.name: Banarasi Lassi
food.desc: Thick set-curd lassi served in an unglazed clay cup, crowned with rabri, malai and chopped nuts. A meal more than a drink.

places.name: Blue Lassi Shop
places.note: Tiny lane shop open since 1925, famous for clay-cup lassi with fruit and rabri.

places.name: Pehalwan Lassi
places.note: Wrestler-style extra-thick lassi that locals rate above the tourist favourites.

places.name: Madhur Milan Lassi
places.note: Handy ghat-side stop for a straightforward, very creamy sweet lassi.

food.name: Thandai
food.desc: Chilled milk ground with almonds, melon seeds, fennel, rose and pepper. Ubiquitous around Holi and Shivratri; ask for the plain version.

places.name: Baba Thandai
places.note: Long-standing thandai counter grinding the masala fresh; the classic Banaras stop.

places.name: Mishrambu Sweets and Thandai
places.note: Neighbourhood sweet shop pouring dependable saffron-heavy thandai year round.

places.name: Badal Thandai
places.note: Old-city hole-in-the-wall known among locals for a rich, nut-forward pour.

landmarks: Dashashwamedh Ghat
Varanasi's liveliest ghat, where every evening the spellbinding Ganga Aarti fills the riverfront with fire, incense, bells and thousands of devotees.
Kashi Vishwanath Temple
Hinduism's holiest Shiva shrine, its gold-plated spire hidden in the old city's lanes, now approached via the grand new riverside corridor.
Manikarnika Ghat
The sacred cremation ghat burning day and night for centuries, where Hindus believe the departed attain moksha, liberation from the cycle of rebirth.
Assi Ghat
The relaxed southern ghat where the Assi river meets the Ganges, beloved for sunrise yoga, morning aarti and its café-fringed traveller scene.
Ramnagar Fort
The Maharaja of Banaras' crenellated 18th-century sandstone fort across the Ganges, housing a wonderfully eccentric museum of vintage cars and royal regalia.
New Vishwanath Temple, Banaras Hindu University
A serene white-marble temple with one of India's tallest towers, rising from the leafy campus of Asia's largest residential university.
Durga Temple (Durga Kund Mandir)
An 18th-century ochre-red shikhara temple beside a sacred tank, dedicated to the fierce goddess Durga and thronged during Navratri festivities.
Tulsi Manas Temple
A modern marble temple marking where poet-saint Tulsidas wrote the Ramcharitmanas, its walls engraved with verses of the beloved Hindi epic.
Bharat Mata Temple
A unique temple enshrining not a deity but Mother India herself, represented by a remarkable carved-marble relief map of the undivided subcontinent.
Sankat Mochan Hanuman Temple
A riverside Hanuman temple where the poet-saint Tulsidas is said to have written the Ramcharitmanas, drawing thousands of devotees daily along with a lively morning market.

train.note: No international trains. Varanasi Junction (Cantt) is the main station, with Banaras station at Manduadih and Pandit Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Junction (formerly Mughalsarai) across the river handling many long-distance services - the last of these is about 20 km away, so check which one your ticket names. Book on IRCTC 60 days ahead; the Vande Bharat to Delhi and the overnight trains from Kolkata are the useful links.

intl.op: private cross-border coach operators — tickets through Varanasi travel agents, no reliable online booking

bus.note: The Kathmandu run is usually sold as a through ticket but in practice means a bus to the Sonauli border, a walk across and a change to a Nepali bus - it takes the best part of 24 hours. Domestic UPSRTC services leave from the Cantt bus stand next to the railway station for Allahabad, Lucknow and Gorakhpur; private coaches are bookable through redBus (https://www.redbus.in/).

ferry.note: There is no scheduled ferry. Rowing and motor boats along the Ganges ghats at dawn and for the evening Ganga Aarti are the classic Varanasi experience but are hired by the hour rather than run to a timetable, and boating is restricted when the river is high during the monsoon.

half.name: Sarnath and the Dhamek Stupa
half.blurb: Just north of the city, the serene deer park where Buddha preached his first sermon, crowned by the massive 5th-century Dhamek Stupa.
